etymology: From free offer (a sincere proffer made without price or partiality) and gospel; the well-meant offer of Christ to all who hear.
biblical_def: The free offer of the gospel, also called the well-meant or sincere offer, is the doctrine that in the preaching of the gospel God genuinely and freely offers Christ and salvation to all who hear, commanding all to repent and believe, and promising life to everyone who comes. This offer is universal in its proclamation and sincere in its terms: the call goes out indiscriminately to sinners of every kind, the invitations are real, and God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls him to turn and live. The Reformed faith holds the free offer together with the sovereign decree of election, without collapsing either into the other. God has from eternity chosen a definite people, and Christ’s atonement effectually secures their salvation; yet the gospel is preached to all, the offer is sincere to all, and the responsibility of every hearer to believe is real, so that those who refuse perish justly by their own unbelief. The two truths are not contradictory but are held in their proper places: God’s secret decree belongs to Him, and the revealed call and offer belong to us, and our duty is to preach Christ freely to all and to bid every sinner come. The dictionary holds the free offer against two errors—the hyper-Calvinism that denies any offer to the non-elect and so chills evangelism, and the Arminianism that grounds the offer in a universal atonement and a sovereign-less grace. The gospel is to be freely offered to all, sincerely and without reserve, and whosoever will may come and take the water of life freely.
webster_summary: The doctrine that in preaching, God sincerely offers Christ and salvation to all who hear, commanding all to believe—held together with sovereign election, against both hyper-Calvinism and Arminianism.

Against hyper-Calvinism, which denies the offer, and Arminianism, which grounds it in universal atonement.

corruption_summary: The free offer is denied by hyper-Calvinism and distorted by Arminianism, which grounds it in a universal, ineffectual atonement.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption on one side is hyper-Calvinism, which, zealous for the decree of election, denies that God offers Christ to the non-elect at all, and so refuses to bid all sinners come. This chills evangelism and contradicts the plain Scripture in which God invites every one that thirsts, commands all men everywhere to repent, and declares that He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked but calls him to turn and live. The free, sincere offer to all who hear is the warrant of all gospel preaching.

The corruption on the other side is Arminianism, which secures the universality of the offer by denying the particularity of the atonement and the sovereignty of grace—teaching that Christ died alike for all and that the offer’s sincerity requires a salvation God equally intends for every man. The dictionary holds both truths in their places: God genuinely and freely offers Christ to all who hear, and the responsibility of every hearer is real; yet election is sovereign and the atonement effectual for the elect. The secret decree belongs to God; the revealed offer belongs to us. Our duty is to preach Christ freely to all, and the door stands open: whosoever will may come and take the water of life freely.
roots_summary: The phrase names the sincere universal offer of Christ, held in harmony with sovereign election and definite atonement.

Its sincerity is grounded in God’s revealed will, not a universal atonement.

etymology: From Latin praeteritio, a passing by, from praeterire, to pass over; the passing-by of the non-elect in the decree of reprobation.
biblical_def: Preterition is the theological term for the first part of the decree of reprobation—God’s sovereign passing by of those whom He has not chosen unto salvation, leaving them in the fallen and sinful condition into which all mankind fell in Adam. Reformed theology distinguishes two elements in reprobation: preterition, the negative act by which God in His sovereign good pleasure passes over the non-elect and does not give them the saving grace bestowed on the elect; and condemnation, the positive act by which He justly ordains them to punishment for their sins. The distinction guards a vital truth: God’s passing by is according to His unsearchable will and not according to any foreseen worse sin in the reprobate than in the elect, for all alike were fallen and deserving of wrath; but the condemnation of the reprobate is always just, grounded in their own real sin, so that God is in no way the author of their sin nor unjust in their punishment. The elect are saved by sovereign grace they did not deserve; the reprobate perish by a justice they did deserve. The dictionary holds preterition as the necessary counterpart of election: if God from eternity chose some unto salvation, He thereby passed by the rest, for the choice of some out of a fallen mass is the not-choosing of others. The doctrine humbles the saved, who can claim no merit, and silences every charge of injustice against God, who owes salvation to none and wrongs none in leaving the guilty to the just reward of their sin. The mystery of preterition is to be received with reverence, not pried into with presumption.
webster_summary: The sovereign passing-by of the non-elect in the decree of reprobation—God leaving them in their fallen state—distinguished from the just condemnation grounded in their own sin.
webster_full: PRETERITION, God’s sovereign passing by of the non-elect.
The negative element of reprobation, distinguished from positive condemnation.
God passes over the non-elect according to His unsearchable will, not foreseen worse sin.
Their condemnation is just, grounded in their own real sin.
The elect are saved by undeserved grace; the reprobate perish by deserved justice.

corruption_summary: Preterition is either denied outright or distorted into making God the author of sin, against the careful balance Scripture requires.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the careful Reformed distinction between preterition and condemnation, which guards God’s justice and sovereignty together. God passes by the non-elect according to His sovereign good pleasure, not because of any foreseen worse sin in them; but He condemns them justly for their own real sin, so that He is in no way the author of their sin nor unjust in their punishment. The elect are saved by grace they did not earn; the reprobate perish by justice they did deserve.

The doctrine is corrupted in two ways. Some deny preterition altogether, recoiling from the hard truth and so denying the sovereignty of God in election, as if His choice of some did not entail the passing by of others. Others distort it, speaking as if God were the author of the reprobate’s sin or condemned men apart from their guilt, a slander Scripture forbids—God tempts no man and condemns none unjustly. The dictionary holds the reverent balance: preterition is sovereign and according to God’s will; condemnation is just and according to men’s sin. The mystery humbles the saved and silences the creature’s charge against the Creator, and it is to be received with worship, not pried into with presumption.
roots_summary: The term names the passing-by of the non-elect, the negative side of reprobation, held with God’s perfect justice.

etymology: From restraint (a holding back, a check) and sin; the work of God’s common grace in curbing the outworking of human depravity.
biblical_def: The restraint of sin is the work of God’s common grace by which He curbs and bridles the outworking of human depravity in the world, holding back fallen men from being as wicked as their corrupt nature would otherwise make them. Though all men are by nature totally depraved—corrupted in every part, dead in sin, and incapable of any saving good—they are not in this life as bad as they could be, because God restrains the full expression of their sin. He does this by many means: through the conscience, which accuses and excuses; through the natural affections of family and neighbor; through the fear of shame and punishment; through civil government, which He ordained to bear the sword against evildoers; and by the direct, secret operation of His Spirit upon the hearts of men, as He restrained Abimelech from touching Sarah and turned the counsel of the wicked. This restraint is not regeneration and works no saving change; it leaves the heart unrenewed and the man still under wrath. But it preserves order in society, makes human life possible, and serves God’s purposes of providence and the gathering of His church. The dictionary holds the restraint of sin as an important part of the doctrine of common grace, guarding two truths at once. It upholds total depravity, for the relative civic goodness of unbelievers is owing not to any soundness in their nature but to God’s restraining hand; and it accounts for the order and good found in a fallen world, which would otherwise be a hell of unchecked wickedness. When God lifts the restraint, as He sometimes does in judgment, giving men over to their sin, the depths of human corruption are laid bare.
webster_summary: God’s common-grace work of curbing human depravity—through conscience, family, government, and His Spirit—so that fallen men are not as wicked as their nature would make them; it upholds total depravity while preserving order.
webster_full: RESTRAINT OF SIN, God’s common-grace curbing of human depravity.
Holds back fallen men from being as wicked as their nature would make them.
Worked through conscience, family, fear, civil government, and the Spirit.
Not regeneration; it works no saving change but preserves order.
When God lifts it in judgment, the depths of human corruption appear.

corruption_summary: The civic goodness of the unregenerate is mistaken for natural soundness, denying total depravity; or God’s restraining hand in society is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the relative goodness found among unbelievers is owing not to any soundness in fallen human nature but to God’s restraining grace. The doctrine guards total depravity against the objection that unregenerate men often live decently and do civic good: they do so because God curbs the full expression of their corruption through conscience, affection, fear, and the sword of the magistrate, not because their nature is partly sound. Lift the restraint, and the same men are capable of every evil.

The opposite forgetfulness ignores God’s restraining hand in society altogether, taking the order and good of a fallen world for granted as if it were the natural state of man, rather than a mercy of common grace. The dictionary holds both truths: man is totally depraved, yet God in mercy restrains sin so that human life and society are possible and His church may be gathered. And it holds the solemn corollary: when God in judgment lifts the restraint and gives men over to their own hearts’ lusts, as Romans 1 describes, the true depths of human corruption are laid bare, and a society once orderly may descend swiftly into open wickedness.
roots_summary: The phrase names God’s common-grace bridling of depravity, which upholds total depravity while preserving the order of a fallen world.

etymology: From the threefold division of the law’s uses; the “third use” (Latin tertius usus legis) is its function as a rule of life for the believer.
biblical_def: The third use of the law is its function as a rule of life for the believer—the moral law, summed in the Ten Commandments and the two great commandments, serving the regenerate as the guide and standard of grateful obedience. The Reformed tradition distinguishes three uses of the moral law: the first, or civil use, restrains sin in society; the second, or pedagogical use, convicts of sin and drives the sinner to Christ as a schoolmaster; and the third, or normative use, directs the believer in the way he should walk. This third use is the chief use of the law for the Christian. Though he is no longer under the law as a covenant of works for his justification, having been freed from its curse by Christ, the believer is not without law to God but under the law to Christ, and he delights in the law of God after the inward man. The law cannot justify him, but it shows him the will of God and the path of holiness; freed from its condemnation, he is now free to love and obey it as a son, not a slave. The dictionary holds the third use of the law as the answer to antinomianism, which casts off the law as a rule of life under the pretense of grace. Grace does not abolish the moral law but establishes it, writing it on the heart in the new covenant, so that the justified believer obeys not to earn favor but out of love and gratitude for favor already received. The law, no longer a covenant of works, remains the believer’s rule, his delight, and the Spirit-empowered pattern of his sanctification.
webster_summary: The moral law’s function as the believer’s rule of life—not for justification, from whose curse he is freed, but as the guide of grateful, Spirit-empowered obedience; the answer to antinomianism.
webster_full: THIRD USE OF THE LAW, the moral law as the believer’s rule of life.
Distinguished from the civil use (restraining sin) and the pedagogical use (driving to Christ).
The chief use of the law for the Christian.
Not under the law for justification, yet under the law to Christ as a rule.
The answer to antinomianism, which casts off the law as a rule of life.

corruption_summary: Antinomianism casts off the moral law as a rule of life, mistaking freedom from the law’s curse for freedom from its guidance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the third use of the law against antinomianism. The believer is freed from the law as a covenant of works and from its curse, justified by faith apart from works; but he is not therefore without law to God. He is under the law to Christ, delights in the law of God after the inward man, and walks after the Spirit that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in him. To cast off the moral law as a rule of life, under the pretense of grace, is the antinomian error grace itself condemns.

The doctrine must be guarded equally from legalism on the other side, which puts the believer back under the law as a covenant of works and makes obedience the ground of acceptance. The dictionary holds the Reformed balance. The law cannot justify, and the believer’s standing rests wholly on Christ’s imputed righteousness received by faith; yet the same grace that justifies also writes the law on the heart and sanctifies, so that the believer obeys not to earn favor but out of gratitude for favor freely given. Grace does not abolish the moral law but establishes it. The law remains the believer’s rule, his delight, and the Spirit-empowered pattern of his growing holiness.
roots_summary: The phrase names the law’s use as the believer’s rule of life—a guide to grateful obedience, not a covenant of works.
roots_lines: Latin tertius usus legis — the third use of the law.

The chief use of the moral law for the Christian.

etymology: From Romans 8:15; the Holy Spirit as He works in the believer the consciousness and assurance of sonship.
biblical_def: The Spirit of adoption is the Holy Spirit considered as He works in the believer the consciousness, liberty, and assurance of sonship—the inward witness by which the adopted child of God knows and enjoys his standing as a son. Paul sets the Spirit of adoption against the spirit of bondage: “For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.” Where the law works fear and the sense of slavery, the gospel, applied by the Spirit, works the free and loving access of a son to a father. The same Spirit beareth witness with our spirit that we are the children of God, giving the believer not only the legal status of adoption but the felt experience of it—the liberty to draw near, the cry of “Abba, Father” rising from the heart, the assurance of the Father’s love. Adoption itself is the act of God’s grace by which He receives the justified sinner into His family and grants him all the privileges of a son, an heir of God and joint-heir with Christ; the Spirit of adoption is the Spirit applying and sealing this blessing to the soul. The dictionary holds the Spirit of adoption as a chief comfort of the believer and a mark of the gospel’s difference from the law. Christianity is not a religion of slavish fear but of filial love; the Spirit who indwells the believer is not a spirit of bondage but the Spirit of the Son, teaching the heart to call God Father, and bearing witness that the trembling sinner has been received into the household and love of God.
webster_summary: The Holy Spirit as He works the consciousness and assurance of sonship—set against the spirit of bondage—teaching the believer to cry “Abba, Father” and witnessing that he is a child of God.
webster_full: SPIRIT OF ADOPTION, the Holy Spirit working the assurance of sonship.
Set against “the spirit of bondage again to fear.”
Works the free and loving access of a son to his Father.
Teaches the heart to cry, “Abba, Father.”
Bears witness with our spirit that we are the children of God.

Rom 8:16

corruption_summary: The believer’s filial liberty is lost back into a religion of slavish fear, or presumed without the Spirit’s true witness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the difference between the spirit of bondage and the Spirit of adoption. Christianity is not a religion of slavish fear, in which the soul cowers before God as a slave before a harsh master, but of filial love, in which the adopted child draws near crying “Abba, Father.” Many believers live still under a spirit of bondage, knowing the law’s fear but not the gospel’s liberty; the Spirit of adoption is given to lead them into the freedom and assurance of sons.

The doctrine must be guarded from presumption on the other side—the false assurance that claims the witness of the Spirit without the Spirit’s true work, or that severs sonship from the holiness and obedience that mark God’s real children. The dictionary holds the genuine doctrine: the Spirit of adoption gives both the standing and the felt assurance of sonship, bearing witness with the believer’s spirit, working the cry of “Abba, Father,” and producing the love and obedience of a true child. This witness is a chief comfort of the gospel and a mark of its grace: the trembling sinner, justified and adopted, is received into the family and love of God, no more a servant but a son and an heir.
roots_summary: The phrase names the Spirit as He seals the believer’s sonship, working filial liberty and assurance against slavish fear.
roots_lines: Greek huiothesia — adoption, the placing of one as a son.

etymology: Latin, “the principle of knowing”; a term of Reformed scholastic theology for the foundation of the knowledge of God.
biblical_def: Principium cognoscendi—Latin for “the principle of knowing”—is a term of Reformed scholastic theology for the foundation or first principle by which the knowledge of God is obtained. The Reformed divines distinguished the principium essendi, the principle of being, which is God Himself, the source of all that is and of all truth; and the principium cognoscendi, the principle of knowing, which is the way that knowledge of God comes to us. They further distinguished the external principle of knowing, which is Holy Scripture, the inspired Word in which God has revealed Himself; and the internal principle, which is the illumination of the Holy Spirit, by whom the truth of the Word is savingly understood and received. The point of the term is foundational and far-reaching: theology does not begin from human reason, philosophy, experience, tradition, or the church, but from the self-revelation of God in His Word. God is known only because He has made Himself known, and supremely in the Scriptures; reason and experience are servants that follow, never the foundation that grounds. The dictionary commends the doctrine of the principium cognoscendi as a precise statement of the formal principle of the Reformation—Scripture alone as the source and rule of the knowledge of God—against every system that grounds theology in autonomous reason, mystical experience, or ecclesiastical authority. The believer knows God truly because God has spoken in His Word and the Spirit has opened his understanding; the foundation of all sound theology is not what man finds out but what God reveals, received by faith through the Spirit-illumined Scriptures.
webster_summary: “The principle of knowing”—the Reformed scholastic term for the foundation of the knowledge of God: Scripture as the external principle, the Spirit’s illumination as the internal, against reason or experience as the ground.
webster_full: PRINCIPIUM COGNOSCENDI, Latin for “the principle of knowing.”
The foundation by which the knowledge of God is obtained.
The external principle is Holy Scripture, God’s self-revelation.
The internal principle is the illumination of the Holy Spirit.
Theology begins from God’s revelation, not from reason, experience, or tradition.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:

Psa 36:9

corruption_summary: Theology is grounded in autonomous reason, experience, or church authority, rather than in God’s self-revelation in Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the knowledge of God begins from God’s self-revelation, not from man. The external principle of knowing is Holy Scripture, the inspired Word; the internal principle is the Spirit’s illumination, by which the natural man, who cannot receive the things of God, is enabled to discern them. Against every system that grounds theology in autonomous human reason, in mystical experience, or in the authority of the church, the Reformed doctrine confesses that God is known only because and only as He has made Himself known in His Word.

The corruption takes many forms. Rationalism makes human reason the foundation and judge of revelation; mysticism makes inner experience the source of the knowledge of God; Rome makes the church and its tradition the ground and rule. Each displaces the true principium cognoscendi. The dictionary holds the Reformation’s formal principle: Scripture alone is the source and rule of the knowledge of God, illumined by the Spirit who inspired it. Reason and experience are servants that follow the Word, never the foundation that grounds it. The believer knows God truly not by what he finds out but by what God reveals, received by faith through the Spirit-opened Scriptures.
roots_summary: The term names Scripture and the Spirit’s illumination as the foundation of the knowledge of God, against reason or experience as the ground.
roots_lines: Latin principium cognoscendi — “the principle of knowing.”

A precise statement of the Reformation’s formal principle, sola Scriptura.
usage: The principium cognoscendi names the foundation of the knowledge of God.

etymology: From general and equity (fairness, the abiding justice of a law); a phrase from the Westminster Confession on the continuing use of the judicial law.
biblical_def: General equity is a phrase drawn from the Westminster Confession of Faith concerning the continuing use of the Old Testament judicial law. The Confession teaches that God gave Israel, besides the moral law, sundry judicial laws which expired together with the state of that ancient people, and so are no longer binding upon nations now, “further than the general equity thereof may require.” The phrase distinguishes between the particular form of Israel’s civil statutes—bound to that nation, its land, and its covenant administration—and the abiding principles of justice and righteousness that those statutes embodied. The particular laws have expired with the Old Testament theocracy; but the underlying equity, the timeless justice they expressed, remains instructive and, where it reflects the moral law, binding. Thus the law that required a parapet on a flat roof to prevent a man falling no longer binds in its letter, but its general equity—that we take due care for our neighbor’s life and safety—abides. The dictionary holds general equity as the Reformed mean between two errors. On one side stands theonomy, which would reimpose the judicial laws of Israel, including their penalties, upon modern states as still binding in their detail; on the other stands an antinomian dismissal that finds nothing of abiding worth in the judicial law at all. The Confession’s wisdom is to honor the moral wisdom of God embedded in Israel’s civil code while recognizing that its particular forms belonged to a particular nation and age. The magistrate is to govern by justice, and the judicial law of Israel remains a rich source of moral wisdom for the lawgiver, in its general equity, though not as a binding code.
webster_summary: The Westminster phrase for the abiding justice of Israel’s expired judicial laws—their underlying righteous principles still instructive—the Reformed mean between theonomy and antinomian dismissal.
webster_full: GENERAL EQUITY, the abiding justice of Israel’s expired judicial laws.
From the Westminster Confession on the use of the judicial law.
The judicial laws expired with the Old Testament state of Israel.
Their underlying equity—timeless justice—remains instructive and binding where moral.
The Reformed mean between theonomy and antinomian dismissal.

corruption_summary: The judicial law is either reimposed wholesale on modern states (theonomy) or dismissed entirely, against its abiding general equity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Westminster distinction: Israel’s judicial laws expired with that nation’s state, yet their general equity—the timeless justice they embodied—abides. The error on one side is theonomy or reconstructionism, which would reimpose the judicial code of Israel, including its specific penalties, upon modern nations as still binding in detail, forgetting that those laws were given to a particular people, land, and covenant administration now passed away.

The error on the other side is an antinomian dismissal that finds nothing of abiding worth in the judicial law, severing the magistrate from the moral wisdom of God embedded in Israel’s statutes. The dictionary holds the Confession’s mean. The particular forms of the judicial law have expired; the underlying equity remains a rich source of moral wisdom for the lawgiver, and where it reflects the moral law it binds still. Paul himself draws abiding principle from the law against muzzling the ox. The magistrate is to govern by justice, instructed but not bound by the letter of Israel’s code, honoring the general equity that expresses the unchanging righteousness of God.
roots_summary: The phrase names the abiding justice of Israel’s expired judicial law, instructive to the magistrate though no longer binding in its letter.
roots_lines: “Equity” — fairness, the abiding justice underlying a particular law.
From the Westminster Confession 19.4 on the judicial law.
The judicial laws “expired” with the state of Old Testament Israel.
Their general equity remains instructive and, where moral, binding.
The Reformed mean between theonomy and antinomian dismissal.
usage: General equity names the abiding justice of Israel’s expired judicial laws.
It is the Westminster mean between theonomy and antinomian dismissal.
It guides the magistrate by the moral wisdom of the judicial law, not its letter.

etymology: From particular (concerning individual things) and providence (God’s governing care); the doctrine that God governs every detail of His creation.
biblical_def: Particular providence is the doctrine that God’s providential government extends not only to the great course of the world in general but to every particular creature, event, and circumstance, down to the smallest detail. Against the deist, who allows a general providence by which God upholds the laws of nature but denies His care for individual things, and against the Epicurean, who attributes all to chance, Scripture teaches that God numbers the very hairs of the head, that not a sparrow falls to the ground without the Father, that the lot is cast into the lap but its whole disposing is of the LORD, and that He works all things after the counsel of His own will. Nothing is too great for His power nor too small for His care; the rise and fall of empires and the falling of a sparrow are alike under His hand. This providence is wise, holy, and good, governing even the sins of men and the malice of devils to serve His purposes, without Himself being the author of sin, and it works all things together for good to them that love God. The dictionary holds particular providence as a chief comfort of the believer and a rebuke to the practical deism of the age. The Christian does not live in a world of chance or of an absentee God, but under the constant, detailed, fatherly government of his God, who orders every circumstance of his life—his griefs and his joys, his losses and his gains—for his good and God’s glory. To believe in particular providence is to rest in the truth that nothing befalls the child of God by accident, but all by the wise and loving appointment of his Father.
webster_summary: The doctrine that God governs every particular creature and event, down to the smallest detail—the falling sparrow, the numbered hairs—against deism and chance; a chief comfort of the believer.
webster_full: PARTICULAR PROVIDENCE, God’s government extending to every detail.
Against the deist’s general-only providence and the Epicurean’s chance.
God numbers the hairs of the head; no sparrow falls without the Father.
Governs even the sins of men to His ends, without authoring sin.
A chief comfort: nothing befalls the believer by accident.
scriptures: Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.
But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
corruption_summary: Deism allows only a general providence and denies God’s care for particulars, leaving the believer to chance and an absentee God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is deism, ancient and modern, which allows that God made the world and upholds its general laws but denies that He governs particular events and cares for individual things—leaving the details of life to chance, nature, or the creature’s own management. Scripture refutes it: God numbers the hairs of the head, not a sparrow falls without the Father, the lot’s whole disposing is of the LORD, and He works all things after the counsel of His will. Nothing is too small for His care nor too great for His power.

The practical deism of the age is the more dangerous because it often coexists with an orthodox confession. Many who would never deny providence in word live as though their lives were ruled by chance, luck, or their own contriving, and meet trouble as though their Father had forgotten them. The dictionary holds particular providence as a chief comfort and a summons to faith. The believer lives under the constant, detailed, fatherly government of God, who orders every circumstance—grief and joy, loss and gain—for his good and God’s glory. To rest in particular providence is to know that nothing befalls the child of God by accident, but all by the wise and loving appointment of his Father, who works even the worst to good.
roots_summary: The phrase names God’s government of every particular thing, against deism and chance, the believer’s comfort in every circumstance.
roots_lines: “Particular” — concerning individual creatures and events, not merely the general course.
Latin providentia — foresight, provision, governing care.
The falling sparrow and the numbered hairs picture its reach.
Governs even sin and evil to God’s ends, without authoring sin.
Set against deism (general-only) and Epicurean chance.
usage: Particular providence is preached against deism and the practical deism of the age.
The falling sparrow and numbered hairs are its classic proofs.
It is held as the believer’s comfort that nothing befalls him by accident.

etymology: From Hebrews 10:20; the way of access to God opened by the flesh and blood of Christ.
biblical_def: The new and living way is the phrase by which the Epistle to the Hebrews describes the access to God opened for believers through the flesh and blood of Christ. “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, by a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.” Under the old covenant the way into the holiest of all was barred; only the high priest entered, once a year, with blood, and the standing veil signified that the way was not yet made manifest. But when Christ died, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from top to bottom, and by His own blood He opened a way of access for His people into the very presence of God. It is a new way, in contrast to the old and obsolete covenant that is passed away; and a living way, for it is opened through the living Christ who, having died, ever liveth, and the way itself is no dead form but a living access through union with Him. By this way the believer draws near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with boldness, because the blood of Jesus has answered for his sin and the great High Priest stands for him within the veil. The dictionary holds the new and living way as a precious summary of the gospel’s access: there is one way to God, newly opened and forever living, consecrated through the torn flesh and shed blood of Christ. It is the answer to every other proposed way—of works, of ritual, of human mediators—for no man cometh unto the Father but by Him.
webster_summary: The access to God opened through the flesh and blood of Christ (Hebrews 10:20)—new, replacing the old covenant; living, through the ever-living Christ—the one way of bold approach to God.
webster_full: NEW AND LIVING WAY, the access to God opened through Christ’s flesh and blood.
“By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh.”
New, replacing the old and obsolete covenant now passed away.
Living, through the living Christ who ever liveth, no dead form.
By it the believer draws near with boldness and full assurance of faith.
scriptures: Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh;
Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
corruption_summary: The one way of access through Christ is rivaled by ways of works, ritual, or human mediators, against the gospel’s exclusive claim.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there is one way of access to God, newly opened and forever living, consecrated through the torn flesh and shed blood of Christ. When He died, the veil was rent and the holiest opened; the believer now draws near with boldness by the blood of Jesus. Against every proposed way of approach to God by works, by ritual, by human merit, or by other mediators, the new and living way is exclusive: no man cometh unto the Father but by Christ.

The corruption is the multiplying of other ways—the sacerdotal systems that interpose a human priesthood and repeated sacrifice between the soul and God; the moralism that would approach by works; the religious pluralism that treats Christ as one path among many. The dictionary holds the gospel’s exclusive and gracious claim. The way is new, not the old expired covenant; living, through the ever-living Christ; and open, so that the trembling believer may enter the holiest itself with full assurance of faith. To add to this way is to deny its sufficiency; to seek another is to find none. Christ is the way, and by His blood the door into the presence of God stands open to all who come by Him.
roots_summary: The phrase names the access to God opened through Christ’s flesh and blood—new and living—the one way of bold approach.
roots_lines: Greek prosphatos — new, freshly slain, recently made; the “new” way.
Greek zōn — living; the way is a living access through the living Christ.
“Through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” — opened by Christ’s torn body.
The rending of the temple veil at the cross signified the opened access.
Exclusive: “no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”
usage: The new and living way is preached as the believer’s bold access to God by Christ’s blood.
Its newness and life are contrasted with the old covenant and dead forms.
Its exclusivity answers other proposed ways of works, ritual, or mediators.

etymology: From Acts 20:27; the entire revealed will and doctrine of God, which the faithful minister must declare.
biblical_def: The whole counsel of God is the entire revealed will and doctrine of God in the Scriptures, which the faithful minister is bound to declare without reserve. Paul, taking leave of the Ephesian elders, testified, “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God,” and on that ground he could say he was pure from the blood of all men. The phrase teaches that the preacher’s duty is not to choose among the doctrines of Scripture, preaching only what is popular, comfortable, or congenial to the age, but to declare the whole—the hard doctrines with the sweet, the warnings with the promises, sin and judgment as well as grace and mercy, the demands of God’s law as well as the comforts of the gospel, election and reprobation, heaven and hell, the cross and the coming judgment. To shun any part of the counsel of God is to fail the trust and to leave the hearers’ blood, as it were, upon the watchman’s head. The whole counsel must also be rightly proportioned, each doctrine given its scriptural weight and place, and held together in the harmony of the faith. The dictionary holds the whole counsel of God as the standard of faithful preaching and the answer to a selective, man-pleasing ministry. The minister is a steward of the mysteries of God, required to be faithful, and a watchman bound to sound the trumpet fully; the church is fed and established not by a few favorite themes endlessly repeated but by the whole revealed truth of God, declared in its fullness, proportion, and harmony, for the building up of the saints unto the glory of God.
webster_summary: The entire revealed will and doctrine of God in Scripture, which the faithful minister must declare without reserve—the hard with the sweet—against a selective, man-pleasing ministry.
webster_full: WHOLE COUNSEL OF GOD, the entire revealed will and doctrine of God in Scripture.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Acts 20:27).
The minister must declare the whole—hard doctrines and sweet, law and gospel.
To shun any part is to fail the trust and leave the hearers’ blood on the watchman.
Each doctrine given its scriptural weight, proportion, and place.
scriptures: For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Eze 3:17
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
corruption_summary: A selective, man-pleasing ministry preaches only the popular and comfortable, shunning the hard doctrines of the whole counsel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the minister’s duty to declare the whole counsel of God, not a selection of it. The temptation of every age is to preach only what is popular, comfortable, and congenial—grace without law, comfort without warning, heaven without hell, the love of God without His holiness and wrath—and to shun the doctrines that offend the hearers or the age. Paul’s example rebukes this: he declared all the counsel of God and so was pure from the blood of all men.

The corruption of a selective ministry is grave, for the watchman who fails to give warning bears the blood of those who perish unwarned, and the flock fed only on favorite themes is left starved and unestablished. The dictionary holds the whole counsel of God as the standard of faithful preaching. The hard doctrines must be preached with the sweet, the law with the gospel, sin and judgment with grace and mercy, each in its scriptural proportion and place, and all held in the harmony of the faith. The minister is a steward required to be faithful and a watchman bound to sound the trumpet fully; the church is built up not by a few comfortable themes but by the whole revealed truth of God, declared in its fullness, to His glory.
roots_summary: The phrase names the entire revealed doctrine of God, which the faithful minister must declare fully, in proportion and harmony.
roots_lines: Greek boulē — counsel, will, purpose; “all the counsel of God.”
From Paul’s farewell to the Ephesian elders (Acts 20).
Bound up with the watchman’s charge to give full warning (Ezekiel 3).
Includes the hard doctrines with the sweet, law with gospel.
To be declared in scriptural proportion, weight, and harmony.
usage: The whole counsel of God is the standard of faithful, full-orbed preaching.
Paul’s “I have not shunned to declare” is its charter.
It rebukes a selective, man-pleasing ministry that preaches only the popular.
